draft.title: Combinatorial identities
card: A combinatorial identity is an equation between counts, such as nCr = nC(n − r). It can be proved by counting the same thing in two different ways.
Example: choosing r people from n to join a team gives nCr ways. Choosing the n − r people to leave out gives nC(n − r) ways. Each team matches exactly one leave-out group, so the counts are equal.
Another identity is nC0 + nC1 + ... + nCn = 2ⁿ. Count all subsets of n items. Each item is in or out, giving 2ⁿ. Sorting subsets by size gives the sum.
The method is to describe one situation, count it two ways, and set the counts equal.
draft.remember: Count one situation in two ways, and the two answers must be equal.

a.q: Which statement is true for every n and r, because choosing r items to keep is the same as choosing which items to leave out?
a.why: Each group of r chosen items matches exactly one group of n − r left-out items, so the counts are equal. nPr counts ordered arrangements, so it is larger in general.
a.clue: Choosing who is in matches choosing who is out.

b.q: A club has 5 members. Counting every possible committee of any size, including none, which number is the total?
b.why: Each member is either on the committee or not, so there are 2 choices for each of 5 members: 2⁵ = 32. This equals 5C0 + 5C1 + ... + 5C5. Using 5² = 25 swaps the base and the power.
b.clue: Each member has two choices: in or out.
